name: Nanoneedle patches

lead: These are small patches whose tiny needles dissolve in the skin, carrying ingredients like hyaluronic acid or acne actives.
People place them over a specific pimple, wrinkle or dark spot, often overnight.

paras: The microscopic needles pass the outer skin layer and dissolve, releasing the active where the patch sits.
Temporary redness, itching or swelling are common after microneedle use; allergic reaction to ingredients is possible.

angle.text: The patch is worn over a pimple, line or dark spot so the active reaches the skin below the surface layer. People use them overnight on specific areas.

lead: Nanoneedle patches, often sold as micro-patches or microneedle patches, are small adhesive patches covered in tiny needles that painlessly pierce the outer skin layer. Skincare products use them to carry actives such as hyaluronic acid, peptides or acne ingredients into the skin, aiming at spot-targeted results such as softer fine lines, calmer blemishes or smoother texture.[1]

Most consumer products rely on dissolving tips: the needles are made of water-soluble material containing the active, and they dissolve in the skin so there is nothing to remove.[1] Microneedle delivery has been studied in medicine since the late 1990s, mainly for vaccines and drugs.[1]

paras: Research describes solid, coated, hollow, dissolving and hydrogel-forming microneedles. Solid ones create pores through which a separate product absorbs; dissolving ones carry the active in the needle material itself; hydrogel-forming ones swell on contact with skin fluid and release their contents.[1] Skincare patches are generally of the dissolving type.

Microneedle concepts date to the 1970s and advanced with microfabrication in the 1990s; a 1998 paper from Mark Prausnitz's group at Georgia Tech showed that microneedles could cross the outer skin layer, and clinical trials of drug delivery began in the 2000s.[1]

Microneedle procedures commonly cause short-lived redness, swelling, itching or pinpoint bleeding, usually settling within about a day; infection or pigmentation changes are linked mainly to non-sterile tools, and allergic reactions to the active or material are possible.[1]

No studies found on commercial cosmetic nanoneedle patches specifically. Related research on microneedling and on microneedle drug delivery, including vaccines and insulin, is summarised in reference literature.[1]

timeline.event: Georgia Tech group reports microneedles penetrating the skin barrier.[1]
